essential: Kramenin at Claridge's is greedy for the millionaire and lets him in; Julius insists the secretary leave the suite entirely.
At gunpoint Julius sizes Kramenin up as an abject physical coward. Kramenin first denies knowing Jane Finn.
Kramenin fears Mr. Brown, has met him without knowing it, and could not recognise him again.
Julius argues that money will get him off as insane, so he will not hang; this convinces Kramenin, who is corrupt himself.
Location given: Astley Priors, Gatehouse, Kent. Kramenin says the girl has lost her memory and that the other girl is there too.
Julius takes Kramenin along so he cannot telephone his friends. The chauffeur George is hostile to Bolsheviks. The terrifying drive with tall tales leaves Kramenin as putty.
At the door Kramenin claims betrayal; Whittington checks 'orders--from him?' and hands over both cloaked girls.
Another man recognises Julius and shoots; Julius fires back and tells Tuppence that Tommy is off to the Argentine. Kramenin is released and flees.
Julius identifies 'Annette' as the real Jane Finn. An ambush follows and Julius's cheek is grazed. Jane drops her accent, admits the fake amnesia and weeps; Julius declares himself her cousin.
Tommy climbs over the back of the car and orders the girls onto the train to Sir James. He snatches Julius's revolver and threatens him. Tuppence trusts him: 'If Tommy’s sure--he’s sure.'
Do not explain Tommy's motive, and do not hint at who Brown is.

essential: The train journey: Jane is terrified ('Five long years!'). Tuppence admits a private suspicion that Tommy shares, but will not name it. Tuppence privately doubts whether simple, honest Tommy can match the arch-criminal.
The evasions: the King's Cross feint, the switch of taxis at Holborn, the collision, and Tuppence butting the 'drunk' at Carlton House Terrace. Sir James revives Jane with brandy.
Jane insists on telling her story at once. Danvers on the Lusitania. Mrs. Vandemeyer is suspicious on the Irish boat. Jane substitutes blank papers and hides the real two sheets in a magazine.
The wink, the attack in the train, and waking behind a screen; the gang plan torture.
She feigns amnesia in French. The quiet, ordinary-voiced man twists her wrist and concludes she is not bluffing. She is made Vandemeyer's 'niece' and calls her 'Aunt Rita'.
Faust pictures in a windowless room. She detects the watcher by the rustle of a dress. She hides the papers behind the Marguerite picture.
Years of surveillance: Ireland, then the Bournemouth sanatorium with a false nurse. She half-hypnotises herself into apathy. The nurse imitates a Paris specialist's tests on her.
Back in Soho she waits on Beresford, knowing about the peep-hole. She hears he is to be killed, shouts 'Marguerite' three times, and distrusted Tommy because he had unhooked a picture.
Sir James insists on going tonight to capture Mr. Brown, saying the house is police-watched and that Brown will enter 'in the guise of a friend'.
Tuppence hesitates and asks him to speak. He argues that only three people touched the brandy and that the photograph never left Julius's possession; Jane protests.
These are Sir James's assertions only. The narrator must not endorse his theory and must not reveal his guilt.

essential: Sir James shows the New York cutting and narrates the alleged murder and impersonation of the real Julius. He explains Vandemeyer's death as Brown's desperate step.
Jane cannot believe it. Tuppence admits her suspicions but cannot see why 'Julius' rescued them.
Sir James explains the rescue as a staged escape. He credits Tommy and worries about him, since 'it takes more than one man and a revolver to hold up Mr. Brown'. He pockets a service revolver.
Jane insists on coming: 'Those papers were my trust.'
Police watch the Soho house front and back. On the stairs Tuppence fancies the recess curtain moved, and senses Brown in the house.
Jane recovers the two sheets from behind Marguerite. Sir James confirms the draft treaty and pockets it, then remarks that no sound in this room reaches the outside.
He says they all feel Brown's presence, then reveals that he is Brown. His face changes, and he outlines the triple-victim plan, himself wounded.
He acknowledges Jane outwitted him and raises the automatic. Julius and Tommy seize him from behind ('caught redhanded').
He looks longest at Tommy ('I might have known'), takes poison from his signet ring, says Ave Caesar, and dies.

essential: Julius's lavish supper on the 30th and its guest list: the American Ambassador, Carter with Sir William Beresford, Archdeacon Cowley, Dr. Hall, Tommy, Tuppence, and Jane as guest of honour.
Julius hands Tuppence a cheque to dress Jane. Tuppence teases him over his proposal, exposing his love for Jane.

The 29th passes quietly. Sir James's death is reported without its manner. The organisation collapses, Kramenin flees, and the documents and diary lead to a settlement. Carter burns the treaty in Soho.
Sir William reconciles with his nephew Tommy, names him heir, and is delighted by Tuppence's 'minx' pertness. The archdeacon is nervous, and Tuppence refrains from smoking.
Tuppence gives Jane the place of honour; Jane's 'tiger lily' gown.
Carter: the suspicion of Julius was instilled by Brown.
Julius: the timing of Tommy's execution order made him realise who Brown was.

Tommy's account: the Marguerite and picture deduction, and his suspicion wavering between Julius and Sir James. The Argentine note for Julius and the letter left for Sir James to see. The 'Twopence' signature as proof. The revolver threat as a message. Hiding in the recess.
Julius reveals the photograph was in Vandemeyer's safe; Tuppence admits that is why she suspected him.
